newsitem.title: USA: Clinton backs longer school year for students.
newsitem.headline: Clinton backs longer school year for students.

text.p: President Clinton, renewing his campaign for national education standards, Thursday endorsed a longer school year for students -- saying it would help them compete with their foreign counterparts.
During a town hall meeting with 160 students, teachers and parents, Clinton was asked if he thought that elementary and secondary students should have a longer school year.

"I have always thought that if you could afford it, it was a good thing to do," Clinton said, adding that the current system of taking the summer months off was created to deal with the farming needs that once drove the nation's economy.
"The only major industrial country with a shorter school year than we have ... is Belgium," he said. "Every other nation in the world with an advanced economy has a longer school year."
"I think on balance its a good thing to do," Clinton said of lengthening the school year.

Discussing teaching math, Clinton noted that "our students may skip over a large number of subjects and touch a large number of subject -- for example in advanced mathmatics, but our competitors in East Asia and in Germany, for example, may study fewer subjects but because they are in school longer they go into much greater depth."
"When they get out of high school they carry a higher level of capacity with them," Clinton said.
He cautioned educators that they needed to know "what to do with the time" if they did extend the school year. "You don't want the kids to get bored," he said.

Extending the school year has been the subject of debate in recent years among educators, with opponents saying many already strapped school districts would face huge expenses air conditioning classrooms. A longer year also would increase the cost of teacher salaries.

During the wide-ranging exchange, Clinton also said he favoured the idea of developing a "V-chip" that parents could use to control what their children are exposed to on the Internet. The device soon will be required for new televisions to let parents limit what youngsters can watch.

"It's technically more difficult with the Internet," Clinton said, noting the new services added virtually each day. "But I think that is the answer. Something like the V-chip for televisions, and we're working on it."
He also announced that he had picked up the support of West Virginia and Massachusetts in his quest to improve the nation's schools by having voluntary national testing.
"This is not designed to put anyone down, but to lift us all up," Clinton said in remarks at Robert C. Byrd High School, named after the state's senior Democratic senator.

Clinton has called for voluntary standardised national tests for fourth grade reading and eighth grade mathematics. Under his plan, the federal government initially would pay the costs of the tests, with the states then picking up the expense of the programme.
Participation would be voluntary, but Clinton hopes for the involvement of every state to ensure that all students are meeting basic standards.

He announced that Republican Govs. Cecil Underwood of West Virginia and William Weld of Massachusetts have agreed to participate in the testing programme. Michigan, Maryland and North Carolina have also pledged to participate.
The effort has drawn bipartisan support as Clinton tries to build on efforts introduced, but never brought to fruition, by Republican Presidents Ronald Reagan and George Bush.
